PUBLISHERS' NOTE.

The extraordinary interest with which the Revised English Version of the New Testament has been received, and the universal desire to form a fair and informed estimate of its value, have prompted the publication of several treatises, critical or explanatory in nature, dealing with the work of the Revisers, its purpose, its instruments, its methods, and its results. While such books may be well suited to the needs of the general reader, the purposes of the student and scholar can be properly served only by the text of the New Testament in the original Greek, collated according to recognized principles of criticism by men of trained judgment and acknowledged ability, from the best sources available at present. Such a work is conveniently provided in the excellent text of Westcott and Hort.

In this edition of the New Testament, prepared by the Publishers at the suggestion of several eminent scholars, the Revised English Version has been arranged to correspond as closely as possible, page for page, with Westcott and Hort's Greek text—the two works being printed on facing pages. This arrangement has made necessary, in the English portion, a partial departure from the order of books adopted by the Revisers, as well as the transposition of a certain passage in the Gospel

INTRODUCTION

TO THE

AMERICAN EDITION.

BY

PHILIP SCHAFF.

———

Merits of the Edition.

THE year of our Lord 1881 marks an epoch in the history of the New Testament. It is the birth-year both of the purest English translation and of the purest Greek text of that little book which contains the inspired message of God's wisdom and love to mankind, and which forms the highest standard of Christian faith and duty.

The coincidence is remarkable. The original and the translation were matured during the same long period through harmonious, though independent, cooperation. The editors of the Greek text were members of the English New Testament Company of Revisers; the English and American Revisers had confidential use of advance proof-sheets of this edition of the Greek text as they proceeded, and their translation conforms more closely to it than to any other printed edition from Erasmus and Beza down to Tischendorf and Tregelles.

The so-called Textus Receptus was announced to the world by the Leyden publishers in 1633, with the bold

viii INTRODUCTION TO THE AMERICAN EDITION.

declaration, "Therefore you now have the text received by all." I venture to introduce the Greek Testament of Westcott and Hort with the modest assertion, "Here you have the oldest and purest text of all editions." It is based exclusively on documentary evidence, and on the most careful comparison of all the ancient sources of the text as they have been collected and made available by the tireless diligence of former editors, especially Lachmann, Tischendorf, and Tregelles. It embodies the results of the combined labors of more than a quarter of a century. It will, of course, not supersede the large editions which contain the whole critical apparatus; but it will take its place at once among the best standard editions of the Greek Testament.

I became personally acquainted with the editors and their work at Harrow, in 1869, and saw them afterwards repeatedly at Cambridge, London, and Peterborough. I formed such a favorable opinion of the value of their labors that I arranged with them and their publisher (Mr. Macmillan) for duplicate plates for an American edition, which is now published by Messrs. Harper & Brothers. This opinion ripened into conviction through constant use, since 1870, of proof-sheets of this text, in my edition of Lange's "Commentary on John" (see the critical notes), in my exegetical lectures, and in my work as a member of the Revision Committee.

Drs. Westcott and Hort are ranked in England among the best Greek and Biblical scholars. Dr. Hort (born 1828; educated at Rugby School and Trinity College, Cambridge) is Hulsean Professor of Divinity at the University of Cambridge (since 1878). He is probably more familiar with the textual history of the Greek Testament than any other

I. SOURCES OF THE TEXT OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.

The original autographs* of the apostolic writings are lost beyond all reasonable hope of discovery, and are not even mentioned by the post-apostolic authors as being extant anywhere, or as having been seen by them.† They perished, probably before the close of the first century, with the brittle paper then in ordinary use (the Egyptian papyrus), like all other ancient writings (with the exception of a few that were accidentally preserved in Egyptian tombs and mummies, or under the lava of Vesuvius at Herculaneum and Pompeii). God has not chosen to exempt the Bible by a miracle from the fate of other books, but has wisely left room for the diligence and research of man, who is responsible for the use of all the facilities within his reach for the study of the Bible. He has not provided for inspired transcribers any more than inspired printers, nor for infallible translators any more than infallible commentators and readers. He wastes no miracles. He desires free and intelligent worshippers. "The letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." The Bible, in its origin and history, is a human as well as a divine book, and must be studied under this twofold aspect. It is the incarnation of God's truth, and reflects the divine-human person

* Autographs, archetypes, handwritten originals.
† On the disputed passage of Tertullian, who speaks of "the very authentic letters of the Apostles," see Scrivener, p. 504 (third edition).

of Christ, to whom it bears witness as the Alpha and Omega, as the Way, the Life, and the Truth. Even if we had the apostolic autographs, there would be room for verbal criticism, since they, like other ancient books, were written as a continuous whole, without accents, without punctuation, without division of sentences or words, without titles and subscriptions, without even the name of the author unless it was part of the text itself.

In the absence of the autographs, we must depend upon copies, or secondary sources. But these are, fortunately, far more numerous and trustworthy for the Greek Testament than for any ancient classic. "In the variety and fulness of the evidence on which it rests, the text of the New Testament stands absolutely and unapproachably alone among ancient prose writings." (Westcott and Hort.)

The sources of the text are threefold: Manuscript Copies, Ancient Versions, and Patristic Quotations.

1. THE GREEK MANUSCRIPTS.

The Manuscripts, or Codices,* are the direct and most important sources. They number now between three and four thousand, counting all classes, and many new ones may yet be discovered.† They differ in age, extent, and value.

* Codex, or caudex, means, originally, the trunk of a tree, stock, stem; then a block of wood split or sawn into planks, leaves, or tablets, and fastened together; hence a book, as the ancients wrote on tablets of wood smeared with wax, the leaves being laid one upon another. The Hebrew manuscripts are in rolls.

† The total number of uncial and cursive manuscripts, including lectionaries, recorded by Dr. Scrivener in his third edition (1883, p. xxx.), amounts to 2094, including 300 cursive manuscripts discovered by Dean Burgon in 1883. But Dr. Gregory in 1890 counted

xiv INTRODUCTION TO THE AMERICAN EDITION.

(with the exception of Greece, Lower Italy, and Sicily) the knowledge of the Greek language disappeared after the fifth century until the revival of learning in the fifteenth, and the Latin Vulgate took the place of the Greek and Hebrew Bible. Some frequently occurring words are usually abbreviated (such as Ɵō = θεός [God], κō = κύριος [Lord], ιō = Ἰησοῦς [Jesus], πνᾱ = πνεῦμα [spirit]).

The manuscripts are divided into two classes, uncial and cursive. The former are written in large or capital letters (litterae unciales or majusculae), the latter in small letters (litterae minusculae) or in running hand. The uncial manuscripts are older, dating from the fourth to the tenth century, and are therefore more valuable, but were discovered and used much later than the cursive ones. Two of them, the Sinaitic and the Vatican, date from the middle of the fourth century. The first is complete, the second defective.

A. Uncial Manuscripts.

The uncial manuscripts are designated (since Wetstein, 1751), for the sake of brevity, by the capital letters of the Latin alphabet (A, B, C, D, etc.), with the help of Greek letters for a few manuscripts beyond Codex Z, and the Hebrew letter Aleph (א) for the Sinaitic manuscript, which was discovered last and precedes Codex A.*

* The present usage arose from the accidental circumstance that the Codex Alexandrinus was designated as Codex A in the lower margin of Walton's Polyglot (Scrivener, loc. cit., p. 75, third edition). A much better system would be to designate them in order of their age or value, which would place B and א before A. But the usage in this case can no more be changed than the traditional division into chapters and verses. Mill cited the copies by abbreviations of their names, e.g., Alex., Cant., Mont.;

INTRODUCTION TO THE AMERICAN EDITION. xv

The uncials are written on costly and durable vellum or
parchment, on quarto or small folio pages of one or two,
very rarely of three or four, columns. The older ones have
no division of words or sentences except for paragraphs,
no accents or ornaments, and very few pause-marks.
Hence it takes some practice to read them easily.

The date and place, which were not marked on manuscripts
earlier than the tenth century, can only be approximately
determined from the material, the shape of the letters, the style
of writing, the presence or absence of the Ammonian sections
(κεφάλαια, "capitula") in the Gospels, the Eusebian Canons
(tables of references to the Ammonian sections, introduced after
340, when Eusebius died), the Euthalian sections in the
Acts and Epistles, and the stichometric divisions or lines
(στίχοι) corresponding to sentences (both introduced by
Euthalius, around A.D. 458),* marks of punctuation (ninth
century), and so on. Sometimes a second or third hand has
introduced punctuation and accents or different readings. Hence
the distinction between readings "by the first hand," marked with an asterisk (*);
"by the second hand" (**, or ², or ᵇ); and "by the third hand" (***, or ³,
or ᶜ).

Some manuscripts (such as Codices C, P, Q, R, Z, Ξ) have been written
over twice, due to the scarcity and cost of parchment,
and are called "codices rescripti," or palimpsests (from the Greek

* The story of the discovery, which made Tischendorf one
of the happiest men I ever knew, reads like a heroic romance.
His three journeys from Leipzig to Mount Sinai, in pursuit of
manuscript treasures, in 1844, 1853, and 1859; his first rescue of
forty-three leaves of the Septuagint from a waste-basket in the
Convent of St. Catharine in 1844; his final discovery of the
whole Codex Sinaiticus in 1859, with the powerful aid of the
recommendation of Alexander II, who met such a terrible death
at the hands of the Nihilists in 1881; his patient labor in
transcribing it at Cairo, and in its publication at Leipzig; his
controversy with the Greek Simonides, who impudently claimed
to have written the codex on Mount Athos in 1839 and 1840—
all of this is told by himself, not without some excusable vanity, in his
Reise in den Orient (1845-46), and Aus dem heil. Lande (1862);
his Notitia Codicis Sinaitici (1860); the Prolegomena to his
editions (1862 and 1865); in his two controversial pamphlets, Die
Anfechtungen der Sinaibibel (1863), Waffen der Finsterniss wider
die Sinaibibel (1863); and most fully in his Die Sinaibibel ihre
Entdeckung, etc. (1871). When, on a visit to Mount Sinai in
March 1877, I saw a copy of the magnificent four-volume edition
in the convent library, and mentioned the name of Tischendorf,
the sub-prior flared up in indignation and called him a
thief, who had stolen their greatest treasure under the pretext of a
temporary loan; and when I reminded him of the large reward
from the Emperor of Russia, who had furnished a new silver shrine
for the coffin of St. Catharine, he admitted it reluctantly; but
remarked that they did not want the silver, but the manuscript
—the manuscript which these monks could not even read, and had
once been ready to throw into the fire! After long delays, the
manuscript was formally presented to the Czar in 1869 in the name of
the new prior, Archbishop Kallistratos, and the monks of the
Convents of St. Catharine and Cairo. Die Sinaibibel, p. 91.

A. Codex ALEXANDRINUS of the fifth century, in quarto and two columns (12¾ inches long, 10¼ wide), given by Patriarch Cyril Lucar of Constantinople (the unfortunate reformer, formerly of Alexandria) to King Charles I. (1628), now in the British Museum, London, where the open volume of the New Testament is exhibited in the manuscript room. It was probably written in Alexandria. It contains on 773 leaves the Old Testament, in the Septuagint Version (edited by Baber, London, 1816-28), and the New Testament; but, unfortunately, with the omission of Matt. i. 1-xxv. 6, John vi. 50-viii. 52, and 2 Cor. iv. 13-xii. 6. It also has at the end the Greek Epistle of Clement of Rome to the Corinthians, with a fragment of a second epistle, or homily. This was the only Greek manuscript of Clement in existence before the discovery by Philotheos Bryennios of the copy at Constantinople (1875). The New Testament portion of the Alexandrian manuscript was published by Charles G. Woide in uncial type (London, 1786), and by B. H. Cowper, in ordinary type (ibid. 1860). We now have it in a most beautiful photographic facsimile, issued by the Trustees of the British Museum, London, 1879. The Old Testament was published in 1882 in the same style.

Codex A is the first uncial manuscript that was used by textual critics. It presents a text that occupies an intermediate position between the oldest uncial text and the later text. It ranks third or fourth among the manuscripts, next to א and B, and perhaps C. On the following page we give two specimens.

Manuscript A favors the reading "of the Lord" over "of God."

It is more accurately written than the Sinaitic manuscript, but not as complete. It dates from the sixth century, and contains only the Gospels and Acts, with a Latin version; edited by Thomas Kipling, Cambridge, 1793, 2 vols. fol., and more accurately by Dr. Scrivener, in common type, with a copious introduction and critical notes, Cambridge, 1864.

The text is very peculiar and puzzling. It has many bold and extensive interpolations, e.g., a paragraph after Luke vi. 4 (which is found nowhere else): "On the same day he [Jesus] saw a certain man working on the Sabbath, and said to him, Man, blessed are you if you know what you are doing; but if you do not know, you are cursed and a transgressor of the law." It differs more than any other manuscript from the received Greek text, but it often agrees in remarkable readings with the ancient Latin and Syriac versions. Alford (i. 110) thinks that it was written in France by a Latin copyist ignorant of Greek. Beza obtained it from the monastery of St. Irenaeus at Lyons in 1562, but did not use it because of its many departures from other manuscripts. Tregelles remarks that "its evidence when alone, especially in additions, is of scarcely any value as to the genuine text; but of the very greatest when corroborated by other very ancient authority."

B. THE CURSIVE MANUSCRIPTS.

The cursive manuscripts are indicated by Arabic numerals. They were written in current (cursive) hand on vellum or parchment (membrana); or on cotton paper (charta bombycina, also called charta Damascena, after its place of manufacture), which came into use in the ninth and tenth centuries; or on linen paper (charta proper), which was first used in the twelfth century. Some are richly illuminated. They date from the ninth century to the middle of the fifteenth century, when the invention of printing provided a much easier and cheaper way of multiplying books. A few, however, were written in the sixteenth century. More than thirty contain the whole New Testament.

Many cursive manuscripts have been collated, in whole or in part, by Mill, Wetstein, Griesbach, Birch, Alter, Scholz, Matthaei, Muralt, Tregelles, Tischendorf, Scrivener, Hoskier, and Gregory.

Their number has greatly increased recently, especially due to the discoveries of Dean Burgon and Dr. Gregory. As a result, the earlier estimates by Tischendorf, Scrivener, and Abbot have been superseded.

Dr. Gregory, in the second part of his Prolegomena (1890), provides the most recent and complete account of the cursive manuscripts. He counts 3553 in total, as follows:

Gospels.......................................... 1273
Acts and Catholic Epistles....................... 416
Pauline Epistles.................................. 480
Apocalypse........................................ 183
Lectionaries (Gospels, 936; Apostles, 265)........ 1201

The critical value of the cursives is, of course, not nearly as great as that of the uncials, because they are much further removed from the original source. But some twenty

2. THE ANCIENT VERSIONS.

Next to the study of the manuscripts, the most important aids
in textual criticism are the ancient versions, or translations
of the Scriptures from the Hebrew and Greek into vernacular
languages. They are, however, only indirect sources,
since we must translate them back into the original, except in

xxxvi INTRODUCTION TO THE AMERICAN EDITION.

sions, there are sometimes ambiguous passages in which a
version may preserve the traditional sense (John i. 3, 9;
viii. 25, etc.), or indicate an early difference of translation;
and then its evidence may be of the highest value. But
even here the judgment must be free. Versions supply
authority for the text, and opinion only for the render-
ing." * It matters comparatively little whether they are
elegant or wretched, so long as they reflect with accuracy
the original text. One service of great importance they
can clearly be depended upon to render—to show where
insertions or omissions occur in the original text before the
translator. It is therefore very weighty evidence against
the genuineness of any particular passage that it is not
found in the most ancient versions.

The most important of these versions are the Syriac, the
Old Latin, the Vulgate, the Egyptian, the Ethiopic, the
Gothic, and the Armenian.

A. Syriac Versions.

met the needs of the Syrian Christians before the un-

has always been a bond of union between the
different sects, who still read it as a sacred classic, although
its language is no longer the vernacular. The Peshito is
the most faithful and accurate of the older versions, and

Notwithstanding its age and value, it was not known to Europe until 1552; and in 1555, at Vienna, the first edition appeared, at the expense of the Emperor Ferdinand I., edited by Albert Widmanstadt, the imperial chancellor. The peculiarity of the Peshito Version, and a proof of its early date, is its omission of 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, and the Apocalypse. These are the Eusebian Antilegomena, or disputed books, which were not generally received in the Church before the final settlement of the canon toward the close of the fourth century. But the missing epistles existed in a Syriac version before the fourth century, and are supplied in modern editions from another version (otherwise unknown), first brought to light by Pococke, and published at Leyden in 1630. The Apocalypse, likewise of unknown origin, was first published by De Dieu, at Leyden in 1627, from a late Indian manuscript owned by Scaliger.

B. Latin Versions.

(a.) The OLD LATIN (ITALA). This version is not found complete; but from the quotations of the Latin fathers, especially those in Tertullian, Cyprian, Lucifer of Cagliari, Hilary of Poitiers, Hilary the deacon or Ambrosiaster, Ambrose, Victorinus, Jerome, Rufinus, Augustine, Pelagius, and in the Apocalypse Primasius, its text can be restored to a large extent. See Hermann Rönsch, Das N.T. Tertullian's, aus den Schriften des Letzeren möglichst vollständig reconstruirt, Leipzig, 1871 (731 pages).

The version is closest in age to the Peshitta, and may be dated to the middle of the second century. It was not the work of one man, nor was it allowed to remain uncorrected by many. Hence the confusion into which the matter has fallen, and the differing accounts of it given by different scholars; some holding that there were many versions before Jerome, citing in proof of this statement Augustine, De Doctr. Christ. ii. 11; others holding that there was only one version, and citing Jerome as proof. But with the simple and natural explanation that there were many revisions of the one old translation, Augustine and Jerome can be reconciled.

The version was made from the Septuagint for the Old Testament; it is literal, rough, and clumsy; the language is the degenerate Latin of the second century, mixed with colloquial and provincial forms. But this mixture soon rendered it unintelligible, and necessitated constant revisions, and eventually, a new and thorough translation from the original languages.

The balance of probability favors North Africa as the place of its origin, because there, rather than in Italy,

(b.) The Latin Vulgate. In the course of time the text
of the Old Latin became so corrupt that a thorough revision
was imperative, and was entrusted by Pope Damasus, in
382, to Jerome (d. 419), the most learned scholar of his
day, and of all the Latin fathers best qualified, by genius,
taste, and knowledge of Hebrew and Greek, for this diffi-
cult task. He began upon the New Testament, and pro-
ceeded cautiously, making as few changes as possible, so as
not to arouse the opposition of those who, as he says,
"thought that ignorance was holiness." But his scholarly
instincts, no less than his convictions of duty toward the
Divine Word, impelled him to go beyond his instructions,
and make a new version of the Old Testament directly
from the Hebrew, of which, however, it does not concern us
at present to speak. Jerome's revision and new translation
(finished 405) encountered much opposition, which greatly
irritated his temper and betrayed him into contemptuous
abuse of his opponents, whom he styled "bipedes asellos"
[two-legged asses]. But, by inherent virtues, rather than by
external authority, it passed into such current use that in
the eighth century it was the Vulgate, the common version,
in the Western churches. It became much corrupted by
frequent copying. Alcuin, at the instance of Charlemagne,
revised it around 802, by the collation of various good
manuscripts, and substantially in this form it passed down
to the invention of printing.

The first book printed was the Vulgate—the so-called
Mazarin Bible (Gutenberg and Fust, Mayence, 1455). Printing, however, fixed errors and gave them wider circulation, and revision was once again felt to be essential.

In the Council of Trent (Dec. 13, 1545, to Dec. 4, 1563) the matter was introduced on Feb. 4, 1546, and the recommendation for revision was passed on April 8; but it was not until 1590, during the pontificate of Sixtus V., that the revised edition of the Vulgate appeared. The scholarly pope took an active interest in the work, rejecting or approving the suggestions of the board of revisers, and corrected the proof-sheets with his own hand. It was prefaced by the famous—and, as events proved, far from infallible—constitution Æternus ille (dated March 1, 1589), in which the pope declared, "By the fulness of apostolic power, we decree and declare that this edition of the sacred Latin Vulgate of the Old and New Testaments, which has been accepted as authentic by the Council of Trent, . . . shall be received and held as true, legitimate, authentic, and unquestioned, in all public and private disputation, reading, preaching, and explanation." He further forbade any alteration whatsoever, ordered that this text, and no other, should thenceforth be printed, and hurled anathemas against anyone who disobeyed the constitution. But alas for the pope! the "immaculate" edition was full of errors and blunders, and no sooner was he dead (Aug. 27, 1590) than demand arose for a new edition. Bellarmine suggested an ingenious though dishonorable way out of the awkward situation in which Sixtus had placed the Church—namely, that a corrected edition should be hastily printed under Sixtus's name, with the blame for the errors thrown upon the printer! His suggestion was adopted, but it was not

D. Ethiopic Version.

There must have been a demand for a translation of the New
Testament very shortly after Christianity entered Abyssinia.
So, although the tradition which assigns it to Abba Salama
(Frumentius), the first bishop, may be unreliable, the version
probably dates from the fourth century, as Dillmann
asserts. This scholar likewise praises the version for its
fidelity and general smoothness. The New Testament has
been edited by Thomas Pell Platt for the British and For-

E. Gothic Version.

It is the work of Ulphilas (311–381, or 313–383), the apostle of Christianity to the Goths, who in the fourth century translated the Old Testament from the Septuagint and the New Testament from the Greek into Gothic. There are seven famous codices of this version: (a) Codex Argenteus, fragments of the Gospels, dating from the earlier part of the sixth century; (b) Codex Carolinus, forty verses of the Epistle to the Romans; (c) palimpsest fragments of five codices (published by Mai and Castiglione, Milan, 1819–39), portions of Esther, Nehemiah, the Gospels, and Paul's Epistles. The best editions of all these fragments are by H. C. von der Gabelentz and J. Loebe: Ulfilas. Vet. et N. Test. Versionis Gothicae Fragmenta quae supersunt (Leipzig, 1836–46), and by E. Bernhardt (Halle, 1875), each equipped with a complete critical apparatus. Stamm's Ulfilas, 7th edition revised by Moritz Heyne, with Grammar and Lexicon, Paderborn, 1878, is the most convenient for students of the language; Bernhardt's is the best for text-critical purposes. See also W. Bessell: Das Leben des Ulfilas und die Bekehrung der Gothen zum Christenthum (Göttingen, 1860). Uppström: Codex Argenteus (Upsala, 1854); Codices Gotici Ambrosiani (Stockholm, 1864–68); Bosworth: The Gothic and Anglo-Saxon Gospels (London, 1874). II. THE VARIATIONS AND TEXTUAL CRITICISM.

1. Origin of Variations.

Given such a vast number of manuscript copies of the New
Testament, there must necessarily be a multitude of variations.
They are partly unintentional or accidental, and partly intentional
or deliberate. Errors of the first kind arise either from
misreading, from mishearing (in the case of dictation), or
from a lapse of memory. Errors of the second kind are
due either to misjudgment, or to an innocent desire to cor-
rect supposed mistakes, to supply what seemed missing, to harmonize
apparent discrepancies, or to willful corruption for sectarian
purposes. Cases of willful mutilation or corruption of the
text are, however, exceedingly rare. Copyists had too
much reverence for the words of Christ and his inspired
apostles to be guilty of such a thing, though in choosing
between conflicting readings they would naturally be
biased by their theological opinions.*

4. CLASSES OF VARIATIONS.

The variations that really affect the meaning may, with Dr. Tregelles, be reduced to three classes—omissions, additions, or substitutions of words and phrases.

(1.) Omissions. These occur very often from homoeoteleuton (ὁμοιοτέλευτον), when two lines or clauses end with the same word or words, which can easily be overlooked. A very important example of this kind is the sentence in 1 John ii. 23: "he who confesses the Son has the Father also" (the same ending as the preceding clause), which is not found in the Textus Receptus, and is italicized in the English Version; but it is supported by א, A, B, C, P, and other authorities, and has been properly restored in the English Revision. Here the older text restores what the later text lost.

(2.) Additions are very numerous in the later manuscripts and in the Textus Receptus, and must be removed according to the oldest and best authorities. They can be divided into several classes.

(a.) Additions caused by transferring a genuine word or passage from one book to another; first written in the margin or between the lines, and then incorporated into the text. These cases occur most often in the parallel sections of the Gospels. They probably began with the Gospel Harmonies, the oldest of which is Tatian's Diatessaron, from the second century. 5. OBJECT OF TEXTUAL CRITICISM.

The textual variations necessitate textual criticism, which has gradually grown to the proportion and dignity of a special branch of sacred learning. It was matured with the discovery and collection of material during the eighteenth century, and reached its height within the last twenty years. It has been cultivated mostly by Protestant scholars—Swiss, German, Dutch, and English. A few Catholics—like Hug and Scholz, Vercellone and Cozza—have nobly taken part in the work; but, on the whole, the Roman Church cares more for tradition than for the Bible, and is satisfied with the Latin Vulgate sanctioned by the Council of Trent. Protestant Bible Societies have been denounced as dangerous and pestiferous by several popes.

The object of textual criticism, as applied to the Greek Testament, is to ascertain and restore, as far as possible, the original text as it came from the pens of the apostolic authors. It aims to show not what they ought to have written, but what they actually did write.

6. CRITICAL RULES.

Since Bengel, Wetstein, and Griesbach, the critical process has been reduced to certain rules, but there is considerable diversity in the mode and extent of their application. The following may be regarded as being sound, and more or less accepted by the best modern critics.

(1.) Knowledge of documentary evidence must precede the choice of readings.

(2.) All kinds of evidence must be taken into account, according to their intrinsic value.

(3.) The sources of the text must be carefully sifted and classified, and the authorities must be weighed rather than numbered. One independent manuscript may be worth two dozen which are copied from the same original. On closer inspection, the witnesses are found to fall into certain groups or families, and to represent certain tendencies. Bengel and Griesbach first arranged them into recensions or families. Westcott and Hort have modified and perfected this system. They distinguish between the Western, the Alexandrian, the Syrian, and the neutral texts.

(4.) The restoration of the pure text is founded on the history and genealogy of the textual corruptions.

(5.) The older reading is preferable to the later, because it is presumably nearer the source. In exceptional cases later copies may represent a more ancient reading.

(6.) The shorter reading is preferable to the longer, because insertions and additions are more probable than omissions. "The shorter reading is to be preferred to the more verbose one" (Griesbach).

(7.) The more difficult reading is preferable to the easier. "The more difficult reading holds the primacy" was Bengel's first rule.

III. THE PRINTED EDITIONS OF THE GREEK TEXT.

The history of the printed text of the Greek Testament may be divided into three periods:

(1.) The period of the unlimited reign of the so-called Received Text, from 1516 to 1750 or 1770.

(2.) The transition period from the Received Text to the Uncial Text, 1770 to 1830.

(3.) The restoration of the oldest and purest text, 1830 to 1881.

(12.) CARL LACHMANN (professor of classical philology
in Berlin; d. 1851): Novum Testamentum Graece et La-
tine, Berol. 1842-50, 2 vols. Compare his article in the
Studien und Kritiken, 1830, No. 4, pp. 817-845. Lachmann had
previously published a small edition in 1831, with various
readings at the end. In the larger edition he was aided
by the younger PHILIP BUTTMANN, who added the appara-
tus of the Greek text, and also published another edition
based on the Vatican manuscript, in 1856, 1862, and 1865.

Lachmann was not a professional theologian, and was not
hampered by traditional prejudice. His object was to re-
store the oldest accessible text, that is, the text of the fourth
or fifth century, as found in the oldest sources then known
(especially Codices A, B, C, the Itala, the Vulgate, and the ante-Nicene fa-
thers); yet not as a final text, but simply as a sure histor-
ical basis for further work of internal criticism. He
gives, with diplomatic accuracy, even obvious writing er-
rors if sufficiently attested—not as coming from the
original writers, but as parts of the textus traditus of the
fourth century. His range of authorities was limited; Codex
Sinaiticus had not yet been discovered, and Codices B and C
had not been critically edited. But to him belongs the credit of
having broken new ground, and of establishing, with the genius
and experience of a master critic, the true basis. He car-
ried out the hint given by Bentley and Bengel, and had the bold-
ness to destroy the tyranny of the Textus Receptus, and to
substitute for it the uncial text of the Nicene age.

Lachmann met with much opposition from the profession-

Tischendorf started from the foundation laid by Lachmann, but applied his principle less rigorously and drew on a much larger number of authorities. He intended to give not only the oldest text, but also the best one, with the help of all available sources. His judgment was influenced by subjective considerations and a very impulsive temperament; hence the frequent changes in his many editions, which he honestly admitted, quoting Tischendorf against Tischendorf—but these changes mark the progress in the range of his resources and knowledge. In his final and best edition he returns again to the uncial authorities, after a temporary shift toward later documents, and gives full credit to his own greatest discovery, the manuscript from the Mount of Legislation [Sinai].

INDEX TO NOTATION.

The notation adopted in this work is used to draw attention
to three classes of passages:

(1.) Passages where it has been found impossible to decide
which of two or more various readings is certainly right.

(2.) Passages containing readings in regard to which some
suspicion is entertained by the editors.

(3.) Passages where interpolations of special interest occur in
certain documents.

In connection with all passages of the first class, alternative
readings are given, which have a reasonable probability of be-
ing genuine. Of these alternative readings, those which on the
whole are the more probable, or the better attested, are printed
in the text as the primary readings; the secondary readings
being distinguished by a notation which varies according as
they differ from the primary readings by omission, addition, or
substitution.
